claims.text: High-temperature mechanical and thermoelastic behavior in RHEAs is governed primarily by severe lattice distortion.
A multi-principal-element composition produces severe lattice distortion in RHEAs.
Severe lattice distortion impedes dislocation motion.
Lattice-distortion-mediated impediment of dislocation motion enhances strength relative to single-principal-element refractory alloys.
Severe lattice distortion enhances thermal stability relative to single-principal-element refractory alloys.
RHEAs possess greater lattice distortion and atomic-scale disorder than conventional pure Mo or Nb.
The random distribution of multiple refractory elements creates severe local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions act as barriers to dislocation motion.
Barriers arising from local lattice distortion increase yield strength.
Barriers arising from local lattice distortion reduce thermal softening.
Chemical disorder in RHEAs affects phonon scattering and consequently their thermoelastic properties.
From room temperature to 1200°C, RHEAs will have higher yield strength than conventional single-principal-element refractory alloys tested identically.
The elastic modulus of RHEAs will decrease more slowly with temperature than that of conventional refractory alloys.
RHEAs may have lower thermal-expansion coefficients than conventional refractory alloys because of increased phonon scattering.
RHEA thermal-expansion coefficients may be less temperature-dependent than those of conventional refractory alloys because of increased phonon scattering.
The proposed mechanism applies to polycrystalline RHEAs with matched grain size and processing history under inert atmosphere up to 1200°C.
The proposed mechanism does not apply to amorphous or nanocrystalline RHEAs.
The proposed mechanism does not apply in oxidizing environments.
Controlling strain rate can minimize creep during the proposed high-temperature tests.

contradictions.description: The thermal-expansion prediction is qualified as merely possible ('may be'), but failure to observe reduced or less temperature-dependent expansion is nevertheless treated as decisive falsification.
